report:
**Conclusion: The evidence is mixed, but the most authoritative review (Cochrane, 2020) found no clear evidence that probiotics shorten the duration of acute infectious diarrhea.**

Your answer of "no" aligns with the current Cochrane systematic review, which concluded: "Probiotics may not affect how long acute diarrhoea lasts" and "There is no evidence that probiotics are effective in treating acute infectious diarrhea" ([Cochrane](https://www.cochrane.org/CD003048/INFECTN_do-probiotics-help-treat-acute-infectious-diarrhoea); [News-Medical](https://www.news-medical.net/news/20201209/Researchers-examine-effectiveness-of-treating-acute-infectious-diarrhea-with-probiotics.aspx)). A 2021 meta-analysis similarly recommended against routine probiotic use, citing heterogeneity and the need for more standardized studies ([Ann Emerg Med](https://www.annemergmed.com/article/S0196-0644(21)00116-5/fulltext)).

However, several other sources report a benefit. A PMC review stated probiotics "have clear beneficial effects in shortening the duration and reducing stool frequency" ([PMC](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6532699/)), and the RACGP reported a reduction of about 25 hours ([RACGP](https://www.racgp.org.au/clinical-resources/clinical-guidelines/handi/handi-interventions/nutrition/probiotics-for-acute-infectious-diarrhea)). Multiple pediatric meta-analyses also found reduced diarrhea duration in children ([PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40739406/)).

The discrepancy likely stems from differences in study quality, probiotic strains, and population (children vs. adults). The Cochrane review's more cautious conclusion reflects concerns about bias and heterogeneity in the underlying trials. So while some evidence suggests a modest benefit—especially in children with specific strains—the best-quality evidence does not clearly support a consistent effect.
